Toggle


India has spent a decade solving the hard part of selling abroad.


Discovery is solved. An Indian brand can reach a buyer in Ohio through a marketplace, a social platform or its own storefront. Logistics is solved enough. Courier export limits have gone up, postal export centres have opened, and a seller in Coimbatore can ship to Manchester without a freight forwarder. The Foreign Trade Policy set a target of 200 to 300 billion dollars in e-commerce exports by 2030, from a base under 10 billion when it was written.


The reach got built but underneath it, how the world pays changed.


##


Wallets have stopped being an alternative


Digital wallets now account for 56% of global e-commerce transaction value, and 33% of in-store spending. That’s from Worldpay’s Global Payments Report 2026, which surveys more than 63,000 consumers across 42 markets. In the United States specifically, wallets are 40% of online transaction value.


Worldpay has stopped calling these alternative payment methods altogether. When something crosses half of all online spend, it isn’t the alternative. It’s the default, making the card form the alternative now.


##


Indian merchants have the wrong mental model, through no fault of their own


Ask an Indian founder what a digital wallet is and they will describe UPI. Reasonably so. India is one of the most wallet-led markets on earth, with wallets at 68% of e-commerce spend, and almost all of that is account-to-account. Money moves between bank accounts. No card is involved.


Now look at the markets Indian exporters actually sell into. In card-led markets like the US, UK and Australia, wallets are mostly funded by cards. 70% of American and Australian consumers fund their wallet with a card. 67% in the UK.


Same word but different machine.


This is why the gap is easy to miss. An Indian merchant looks at their international checkout, sees that cards are accepted, and concludes they’re covered. And they are, for the payment. The card behind the wallet is the same Visa or Mastercard that would have gone through the card form.


What they’re not covered for is the habit.


##


The habit is the whole thing


A buyer who uses a wallet for everything does not experience a card form as difficult. They experience it as unnecessary. There is no error message, no failed transaction, no support ticket. They put the phone down, and nothing in your analytics tells you why.


That’s the part worth sitting with. The merchant has already paid for the ad, the content, the shipping promise and the trust. All of it works. The buyer arrives at the checkout intending to buy. And the transaction ends before a payment is even attempted.


Worldpay has a term for the underlying shift: glocalization. Consumers expect their local payment method to work everywhere they shop. Card networks were built for international use from the start. The payment methods growing fastest were built domestically first and are only now learning to travel.


Indian exporters are standing exactly where that gap opens.


##


What went live


Google Pay is now live on Cashfree’s International Payment Gateway. Buyers in the US, UK, UAE and Australia can now pay with Google Pay at an Indian merchant’s checkout, alongside Apple Pay, PayPal and cards.


For merchants, nothing changes structurally. Google Pay is part of IPG, not a separate product. There is no new SDK and no separate arrangement with Google. Cashfree handles certification and domain verification. Settlement stays T+2 in INR with FIRS generated automatically. Pricing is unchanged at 2.99% flat.


Merchants on Cashfree Checkout will find it in their existing checkout. Merchants running a custom checkout can switch it on with one setting.


##


The question has changed


For most of the last decade, the cross-border payments conversation in India was about access. Can an Indian business accept money from a customer in another country, and can it do so within RBI’s rules.


That question has been answered. 170 countries, 140 currencies, four licences, automated compliance documentation.


The next question is narrower and harder. When that customer arrives, does the checkout make sense to them?


Reach gets a buyer to the payment page. Familiarity is what gets them through it.
